lessons.title: Minimal state and immutability
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of immutable state updates in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of immutable state updates.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Each render receives an immutable state snapshot; calling the setter asks React for a new render with a new value. Modified objects must be recreated while unchanged ones are reused so references precisely identify changes. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: immutable state updates is like a dashboard where one gauge owns the truth and every other display is calculated. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

Minimal state contains only information that changes and cannot be computed from props or other state; totals and item counts are derived values. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

map creates a new array and spread creates a new object only for the targeted row; mutating item.quantity preserves a misleading reference. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

The functional setter receives the latest snapshot, protecting rapid clicks and updates batched by React. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

objectives: Build an accurate mental model of the value → validation → submission cycle.

blocks.text: In a controlled field, React owns the value and every onChange proposes the next value. Validation is a function of that value; submission reads a coherent snapshot, validates again on the server, and clearly announces success or field errors. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: the value → validation → submission cycle is like a dashboard where one gauge owns the truth and every other display is calculated. value and onChange remain paired; value without onChange makes the field read-only, while switching from undefined to string causes a controlled/uncontrolled change. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

An error derived from query needs neither state nor useEffect; it recalculates during render and cannot become stale. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

lessons.title: useEffect, dependencies, and cleanup
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of synchronization with an external system in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of synchronization with an external system.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: React computes JSX and commits the DOM; only then does an effect synchronize that render with localStorage, a timer, a subscription, or an imperative API. Before the next effect or unmount, cleanup reverses exactly what the previous run installed. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: synchronization with an external system is like a dashboard where one gauge owns the truth and every other display is calculated. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

lessons.title: Context and custom hooks

objectives: Build an accurate mental model of controlled sharing of cross-cutting state.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Context broadcasts a value from a Provider to descendants without manually passing every level. A custom hook encapsulates reading, verifies the Provider exists, and exposes a stable domain API rather than internal state details. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: controlled sharing of cross-cutting state is like a dashboard where one gauge owns the truth and every other display is calculated. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

Context fits truly cross-cutting values such as cart, session, or theme; state used by two nearby siblings can simply move to their parent. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

A null default forces useCart to detect missing configuration instead of silently returning a fake empty cart. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

The hook hides useContext and protects consumers from future implementation changes; they learn add and count, not setState. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
